name: K'iche', Eastern
confidence_why: The judge's premise that Wood 2025 agrees with Henderson 2012 on main-stress placement is wrong: Wood 2020/2025, the only first-hand description of the record's own Chichicastenango (Eastern) dialect, states that this dialect differs from the others in the distribution of stress, with final stress in non-verbs but vowel-quality- and weight-sensitive stress in verbs (kaˈwesaj 'you remove it', xuˈch'omaj 'he thought', where Henderson's and Barrett's rules put stress on the final heavy syllable), so the record's fixed: final syllable coding is contradicted in placement for a major word class by the dialect's sole source, while the rule string's alternating secondaries rest on an uncited Wikipedia sentence; final stress in non-verbs is secure across every source, so the answer is known in outline, but the disagreement is real, not a detail.
readall_conflicts: The one listed work could not be opened, so nothing new was read from it. Among sources already held by the project in our check folder (opened here only to ground this paragraph): Wood 2025 (JIPA 55, lines 202-206, printed p.468) states that in Chichicastenango K'iche' verbs 'Stress falls on the left-most syllable containing either a tense vowel or a coda, or if there are none, on the final syllable' with the stress domain excluding most inflectional morphemes, while non-verbs are word-final with the extrametrical suffixes -alaj and -ik (p.467, per the folder's); this is a weight/quality-sensitive refinement of plain final stress for exactly the Eastern variety. The catalog alternating stress from the right also encodes alternating (iambic) secondary stress, which the folder's traces to an unreferenced Wikipedia sentence; Henderson 2012 (preprint the text) says uneven-weight forms 'pose a problem for iambic treatments of K'ichee' stress', and Wood 2020 (kich1263 folder, p.88) reports no description of secondary stress in the Chichicastenango dialect. So the primary-stress placement (final) agrees across sources, but the secondary-stress component of the catalog rule is unsupported by the primary descriptions held by the project, and the Eastern variety's verb stress is more complex than fixed: final syllable.

sources.citation: Nielsen, Kuniko. 2005. Kiche intonation. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 104:45-60.https://escholarship.org/uc/item/52n7344j(downloaded via web.archive.org)
sources.quote: 'Stress in Kiche is always word-final (Larsen, 1988). Stressed syllables are marked by pitch, duration, intensity, and loudness. Most importantly, Kiche stress is marked by a rise of the fundamental frequency (F0) on the stressed syllable.' 'Only when an AP has more than 3-4 syllables, the first syllable (often determiners) is realized as H* (= rhythmic high).' One speaker, instrumental; no word-level alternating secondaries reported.
sources.locator: p. 45; p. 48 (pitch accents); speaker = Cantel dialect (West Central)
sources.note: Instrumental (one Cantel speaker): confirms word-final primary stress cued by F0 rise; reports only an AP-initial 'rhythmic high', no iambic alternation.

sources.quote: 'In K'ichee' roots and stems, word-final CVC and CVV syllables receive primary stress. Secondary stress occurs in words of three or more syllables and falls on the initial syllable and consecutive alternating syllables moving left to right. Secondary stress does not occur on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable (i.e. stress clash between secondary and primary stress is not allowed).' Examples: tìnamít, k'òlok'ík, ètamab'ál, kàwunùnwutík, tìkoonijél, xìnts'ib'àapaník. 'The primary stress is actually a moraic trochee aligned at rightmost edge.
